tip_title: Your Home Policy Renews Every Year. Does It Still Reflect Your Actual House?
topic: Homeowners Insurance Annual Review — Policy Update Triggers
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: Your Home Policy Renews Every Year. Does It Still Reflect Your Actual House?**

Most homeowners set up their coverage when they buy the house and then let it auto-renew without a second look. The problem is that your policy doesn't automatically update when your life does. A finished basement, a new kitchen, a security system, a fence — none of that gets reflected in your coverage unless you tell your insurer it's there. The same goes for new valuables like electronics, jewelry, or furniture. If your dwelling limit was calculated based on what your house looked like five years ago, it may not cover what it would cost to rebuild it today, especially with where construction costs have gone. Annual renewal is the natural moment to spend ten minutes checking whether the coverage still matches the house.

Not sure where to start? Your Peachy agent can pull up your declarations page and walk through whether anything needs updating — usually a quick call.

📖 [Learn more from the NAIC](https://content.naic.org/article/consumer-insight-searching-homeowners-insurance-policy-tips-get-most-value)
summary: Covers the homeowners insurance annual review as a recurring action item, focused on updating dwelling coverage and personal property limits after home improvements or new purchases — distinct from prior renovation-specific tip by framing it as a broad annual renewal habit rather than a post-project trigger.
scoring_notes: Prior renovation tip ('Did You Renovate? Your Home Policy Might Not Know That Yet,' April 2026) was specifically framed around post-renovation underinsurance. This tip is framed as a general annual renewal review habit — the trigger is the renewal itself, not a specific project — and includes a broader set of update categories (security systems, valuables, fencing, lifestyle changes) beyond just renovations. Angle is meaningfully different: recurring habit vs. one-time project event. High homeownership rates across all three newsletters (East Cobb 78%, Lewisville Lake 65%, Perimeter 55%) make this relevant to a large share of combined readership. Evergreen with a slight seasonal hook: many policies renew mid-year, and summer is a common time households complete projects. Source is NAIC — on the trusted list. Forbes and NerdWallet candidates dropped in favor of NAIC for source trust.

tip_title: There Are Now Two Ways to Buy Flood Insurance. Most People Only Know About One.
topic: Flood Insurance — NFIP vs. Private Insurer Comparison
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: There Are Now Two Ways to Buy Flood Insurance. Most People Only Know About One.**

For a long time, if you wanted flood coverage, you went through the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) — full stop. That's still an option, and it's still the most common one, but private insurers now offer flood policies too, and the differences matter. Private policies often include things the NFIP doesn't — like replacement cost coverage for your personal belongings or loss-of-use coverage for temporary living expenses if your home becomes uninhabitable after a flood. The NFIP uses community-level flood maps to set rates; private insurers can assess the specific risk of your individual property, which sometimes works in your favor and sometimes doesn't. Neither option is automatically better — it depends on your property, your flood zone, and what coverage you actually need.

If you already have flood coverage and haven't compared options recently, or if you've been putting off getting it, your Peachy agent can walk through both paths with you.

📖 [Learn more from the NAIC](https://content.naic.org/article/consumer-insight-understanding-flood-insurance-and-what-do-during-flood)
summary: Covers the comparison between NFIP and private flood insurance options — specifically what each includes and excludes, and how each prices risk — framed as an educational overview of a choice most consumers don't know exists.
scoring_notes: Prior flood coverage was 'Your Home Policy Doesn't Cover Flooding. Here's What Does.' (June 14) — that tip established the existence of flood insurance and the NFIP. This tip takes a substantively different angle: the NFIP vs. private insurer comparison and what each actually includes, particularly the coverage features (replacement cost for contents, loss-of-use) that NFIP lacks. New angle clearly stated. July is peak Atlantic hurricane season, and the Lewisville Lake area (north Texas) sees significant storm and flash flood activity in summer. East Cobb and Perimeter are both in the greater Atlanta metro, which has meaningful flood exposure. Homeownership rates across all three newsletters (55-78%) mean a large share of readers have a stake in this. Source is NAIC — on the trusted list.

tip_title: Your Car Might Be Earning You a Discount Right Now — You Just Haven't Asked
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: Your Car Might Be Earning You a Discount Right Now — You Just Haven't Asked**

Usage-based insurance (UBI) programs let your driving behavior — things like how often you brake hard, what time of day you drive, and how many miles you log — actually work in your favor on your premium. If you're a low-mileage driver or someone who doesn't spend much time on the road during high-risk hours, you're basically leaving money on the table by staying on a standard rate. Most programs use either a mobile app or a small plug-in device, and many carriers give you a discount just for signing up, before they've even tracked a single trip. Worth a five-minute conversation to see if it fits how you drive.

Not sure if your current policy has a program like this? Ask your Peachy agent — they can check what's available and whether your driving profile is a good fit.

📖 [Learn more from the Insurance Information Institute](https://www.iii.org/article/how-usage-based-insurance-works)
summary: Covers usage-based auto insurance programs that reward low-mileage or low-risk drivers with premium discounts, framed as an overlooked savings lever worth asking about rather than a standard discount list.
scoring_notes: No prior coverage of UBI discounts in the history. Auto category is underrepresented this week after the teen driver and road trip tips aged out. Hits all three newsletters: East Cobb and Perimeter audiences skew commuter-adjacent, and Lewisville Lake has a significant young professional and college-adjacent segment that drives less. July timing works — summer travel patterns shift mileage for many households, making this a natural moment to ask the question. Source (U.S. News) is not on the trusted list, so swapping the learn-more attribution to III which covers UBI directly. Source candidates from thezebra.com and valuepenguin.com dropped — not on trusted source list.
